Matched task · 32 paired dictionaries · Two full-weight learners · 2026-09-06

Does the Zipf learning curve survive training the weights?

Ranked observations produce faster finite learning curves in both fine-tuned models.

We replaced storage in the prompt with full-weight fine-tuning while retaining the original dictionaries, example streams, oracle labels and weighted test items. The experiment distinguishes how observations are acquired from how the learner stores them.

Effective exponents fit error ∝ N⁻ᵝ over the five prespecified budgets 8, 16, 32, 64 and 128. Brackets are 95% intervals from 1,500 paired whole-dictionary bootstrap samples. These finite-range slopes do not establish asymptotic scaling laws or exponent equivalence.

Query generation: a decoder bias and a corrected pilot

Qwen3-0.6B: final error with its own generated queries is higher relative to IID study; paired error difference 0.559 [0.493, 0.626]. SmolLM2-135M: final error with its own generated queries is higher relative to IID study; paired error difference 0.680 [0.619, 0.732].

The current fine-tuned model greedily emits a legal key and guesses its label before feedback. Its prompt explains the rank frequencies and lists previously requested IDs, with no correct-label history. Each request costs one label, including repetitions. Decoding constrains valid IDs but does not enforce useful choices, novelty or sorting. A block is acquired before any of that block's labels update the model.

The original decoder has a material limitation. Requiring EOS after the integer biases the models toward continuing the number. With unchanged weights and no feedback, Qwen repeatedly chose 10000 and SmolLM repeatedly chose 12345. Allowing a newline at a legal integer boundary changes both models' choices to repeated key 1. Thus the original generated-query curves combine termination bias with the policy's behavior.

We then allowed newline or EOS and ran actual feedback and weight updates in four fresh dictionaries per model, seeds 52000–52003. This follow-up retained the prompt, legal key prefixes, chosen learning settings and repeated-query costs. It used no held-out test predictions or exponent fitting. The acquisition-calibration requirement was to exceed the exact expected IID coverage at 128 labels in every pilot: 0.8161 of test probability mass.

Mechanism: coverage and retention

For independent four-way labels, an unobserved key contributes expected error 3/4. Thus coverage error is exactly (3/4) × unobserved probability mass. We also enumerate every acquired key to measure its actual test-weighted mistakes. Their sum marginalizes unknown labels and explains the raw test curve without replacing the primary measurement.

Qwen3-0.6B: ranked observed-key error mass is 0.0514 at 8 labels and 0.0000 at 16; its ranked exponent over 16–128 is 0.512 [0.470, 0.551]. SmolLM2-135M: ranked observed-key error mass is 0.0000 at 8 labels and 0.0000 at 16; its ranked exponent over 16–128 is 0.501 [0.473, 0.528]. Optimization transients and finite test sampling can shift fitted slopes away from the exact toy; the primary 8–128 fits remain unchanged.

Actual weight control: in the prospectively selected dictionary 4000, replaying each original live model's identical correct observations and minibatches while omitting generation reproduced every checkpoint probability and every saved parameter tensor exactly, for both model families. This checks the implementation on one paired world per family; it is not another independent replication.

The explicit true weights belong to the linear toy. Transformer parameter-displacement norms are retained in the downloadable data; their magnitudes do not identify alignment with a unique teacher parameter vector.

Exactly what was trained

Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B-Base and HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-135M are reset to the same pretrained revision for every dictionary and arm. We update all model parameters using AdamW, FP32 parameters and state, BF16 autocast, zero weight decay and norm-1 gradient clipping. The loss is cross-entropy over the four ordinary LM output tokens for A/B/C/D. There is no added classifier head. Evaluation supplies only Dictionary key: k\nLabel:, with no association examples.

Each new oracle observation enters a multiset buffer. Each of its R updates uses 32 presentations: the newest observation plus 31 uniform replay draws, including duplicates. Replay index sequences and resets are paired across arms. At N labels this costs RN updates and 32RN training presentations.

Within a model, these training budgets are exactly matched across acquisition arms. A presentation has different computational cost in the two architectures. Because R is fixed within each model, a power-law fit against updates or presentations has the same exponent as its label-budget fit; this change of units is not an independent scaling result.

Fit sensitivity and limits

The 8–128 window was fixed before confirmation. The two additional windows are sensitivity checks on overlapping data. Log-error residuals below expose curvature that a single exponent can hide. Intervals are pointwise and unadjusted for multiple contrasts. The 32 dictionaries are reused from ICL, enabling paired comparisons but not an independent draw of task worlds.

The earlier ICL models emitted 40 answers together in a context containing examples. The fine-tuned models answer each of those same weighted test items independently. They are smaller base models, not the original hosted instruction-tuned models. These differences limit a causal comparison of ICL versus weight storage.

Scope of the conclusion: this tests acquisition and coverage with verified feedback. Ranked study and model-generated practice can supply the same information. It does not isolate a benefit of producing an answer, distinguish generative and discriminative architectures, or demonstrate learning from unverified self-generated labels.

Reproducibility and resources

All 256 model/dictionary/arm runs and 2,304 checkpoints were independently regraded from saved probabilities. Curricula, target labels, replay causality, paired resets and source hashes were checked. Eight preselected final models were archived to the configured shared cache, with SHA-256 verification of every copied file. All dictionaries retain their predictions, acquisition records and replay indices.
